measurement.happened:
This week in China was dominated by a cultural storm that spilled into politics, a major internal party gathering, and a deepening economic malaise that is now visibly hurting the global auto industry.

The Mbappé–Mao scandal was the loudest story. Kylian Mbappé, in what appears to have been a casual remark or meme reference, called Mao Zedong a 'Chinese dictator,' and the comment went viral on Chinese social media. The backlash was swift and punishing: Real Madrid issued a formal public apology to the Chinese people, La Liga suspended scheduled matches, Mbappé's Chinese sponsors (including major brands) dropped him, TV broadcasts of his games were halted, and the French football federation eventually backed him after the dust settled. China's official response was to say it took the apology 'seriously,' a carefully measured phrase that signaled the matter was now a quasi-state affair. The episode was not isolated: Sanrio, the Hello Kitty maker, cut ties with a Japanese spy-drama TV show after Chinese netizens felt the show mocked China, showing how quickly cultural content can become a diplomatic irritant. Across at least ten sources and nearly a dozen headlines, the Mbappé story was the single most-covered item of the week, and commentators from Bloomberg to TV5Monde framed it as a sign of China's growing power to punish foreign brands and celebrities for perceived slights. (Sources: Reuters, AP, AFP, BBC, CNN, Deutsche Welle, TV5Monde, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Al Jazeera.)

The Communist Party's fourth-quarter plenum, held around October 26–29, was the week's other major domestic story. The gathering focused on tightening party discipline, and the outcome included the record expulsion of 33 officials and a notable number of absences, which analysts read as a sign of ongoing purges. A striking personnel decision was the elevation of Zhang Shengmin, the general who led the anti-corruption sweep in the military, to the Politburo, a rare move that signals Xi's desire to keep a trusted enforcer close to the top. Xi used the plenum to demand greater loyalty from the party elite, and the BBC, AP, WSJ, and FT all framed the meeting as a consolidation of power and a signal that the hunt for the next generation of leaders is being reshaped by the purge. (Sources: Reuters, AP, BBC, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, TV5Monde, CNBC.)

The economic picture was grim. China's factory activity, as measured by the PMI, contracted in October for the third time in four months, with new export orders weakening. This was not an isolated data point: Volkswagen posted its deepest quarterly loss since the Dieselgate era, Audi cut its 2026 outlook, Mercedes-Benz slashed its profit guidance, Toyota's China sales fell for the eighth straight month, and Carlsberg, Haleon, and Reckitt all cited weak Chinese demand. Chinese EV makers like BYD and Geely are offsetting domestic softness with surging exports, but the WSJ and CNBC noted that Chinese electric carmakers are running out of domestic buyers. Local governments are saving more but are too fearful to spend, and the FT described an 'AI bubble' that has already popped in China while the broader consumer slump demands what one analyst called a Japan-style stimulus response. (Sources: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, Deutsche Welle, AFP.)

US–China tech and trade friction accelerated. The FCC voted to ban all Chinese laboratories from testing US electronics. The US Treasury moved to limit Chinese biotech deals while still allowing licensing. Three Chinese genomics companies were banned over forced-labor allegations, and China condemned the US for adding Chinese medical-equipment firms to the Uyghur forced-labor list. The US also planned to ban Chinese telecom firms from direct access to US phone numbers and hit Chinese truck trailers with tariffs. China warned of retaliation over the test-lab restrictions. Meanwhile, China made its first inquiry for US wheat since the Trump–Xi summit, a small but notable thaw in a specific trade lane. (Sources: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC.)

The Nvidia spy-plot story generated significant attention. Reports surfaced that a Chinese executive close to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was suspected of passing information to Beijing. Trump said the US was looking 'closely' at the report. China denied any spying operation, and Nvidia itself said the diversion allegations had been 'investigated and debunked.' The episode fed into a broader narrative about US–China competition for AI dominance, with the AP noting that countries are increasingly torn between the two AI blocs. (Sources: Reuters, AFP, BBC, Bloomberg, WSJ, CNBC.)

Maritime and border tensions continued. China's coast guard conducted patrols east of Taiwan, and Taiwan's military flagged an 'obvious' threat from 50 Chinese vessels in a wide sweep of waters. China also conducted combat-readiness patrols around a disputed shoal in the South China Sea, and tensions with the Philippines resurfaced at the close of an ASEAN defense gathering. In the South China Sea and around Taiwan, China was reported to be collecting data that could aid its forces. On land, India–China border face-offs continued to test the relationship, and India approved 22 billion dollars in military spending partly in response. (Sources: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, WSJ, Al Jazeera, CNBC.)

Diplomacy was active on several fronts. Xi met German leadership and urged a 'pragmatic' policy toward China, while German President Steinmeier visited Beijing and said China must avoid one-sided benefits. China signed a trade accord with Switzerland that bucks the global trend toward protectionism, and Swiss firms announced plans to boost investment in Chinese drug and finance sectors. The upgraded China–Peru trade deal took effect. Kim Jong Un made a surprise visit to China, crossing a newly inaugurated cross-border bridge, and North Korea fired missiles days after the trip. An Australian PM was set to visit Beijing after an APEC meeting. (Sources: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, Deutsche Welle, CNN, Al Jazeera.)

On the tech and science front, China's chip maker CXMT reported its first quarterly profit after Asia's biggest IPO of the year and began production of advanced AI memory despite poor yields. China issued new export curbs around its AI crown jewels. A Chinese AI model carried out complex cyberattacks in controlled tests. Meta was reported to be building a humanoid robot with Chinese startup Fourier. China's clean-tech exports were estimated to cut global emissions by a Brazil-sized amount in 2026. China also upended global drug development with cheap and rapid human trials, and Bayer got Chinese approval for a stroke-prevention drug. (Sources: Reuters, Bloomberg, WSJ, FT, CNBC, AP.)

In markets and investment, Chinese tech stocks lost their shine amid a sell-off, Chinese investors sought shelter in long-bond ETFs as stocks sank, Hong Kong stocks lost a key backer as Chinese investors headed for exit, and Chinese junk dollar bonds headed for their worst week in a year. The Evergrande property-management arm was sold to an Asian private-equity firm for 514 million dollars, a rare win for creditors. (Sources: Bloomberg, CNBC, WSJ, FT.)
measurement.expected:
Mbappé and cultural fallout: It is almost certain that the Mbappé/Real Madrid/La Liga saga will continue to generate headlines in the coming days, with Chinese social media still processing the apology and possibly more foreign brands or athletes being scrutinized for past remarks. The Sanrio/Hello Kitty episode may also draw a second wave of commentary. The TV5Monde debate segment ('on ne peut plus rien dire') suggests the conversation is not over. Probable: a few more minor brand or celebrity stumbles as Chinese netizens keep the spotlight on. Possible: a formal Chinese trade or cultural body issuing a soft statement about 'mutual respect' in cross-border partnerships.

Party politics and purges: Almost certain that the plenum's decisions will continue to be dissected by state media and foreign analysts over the next week. Probable: additional names being added to the list of expelled or investigated officials as the 'discipline' campaign rolls out. Possible: further personnel moves in the military or provincial party committees as the Zhang Shengmin elevation sets a precedent. Unlikely: a major leadership shakeup or a surprise resignation at the Politburo level within seven days.

Economic data and stimulus: Probable that more weak economic data will be released (retail sales, fixed-asset investment, possibly a follow-up on the PMI). Possible that the government will signal or deploy a modest stimulus package, perhaps in the form of local-government bond issuance or a targeted consumer subsidy, to counter the 'Japan-style deflation' narrative. Almost certain that European and Japanese automakers will continue to report China-related weakness in earnings calls. Possible: a PBOC liquidity injection or a small rate cut to steady markets, though this is less certain given the current policy stance.

US–China tech and trade: Probable that China will issue a formal retaliation or at least a pointed statement in response to the FCC lab ban, the biotech restrictions, and the telecom phone-number ban. Possible: additional Chinese export controls on rare earths, gallium, or specific AI components as a counter-punch. Unlikely: a full trade-war escalation or new tariffs in the next week, but the tension will keep simmering.

Nvidia spy plot: Probable that the story will continue to generate headlines as both sides manage the narrative. Possible: a Chinese official or state media piece pointing to the 'investigated and debunked' language as evidence of US overreach. Unlikely: a formal US investigation or indictment within the week, but the political pressure is building.

Taiwan and South China Sea: Almost certain that China's coast guard will continue its patrol pattern east of Taiwan and around disputed shoals. Possible: another incident or a new round of warship transits through the Taiwan Strait. Probable that the Philippines will make a new statement or move at the South China Sea, especially with the defense chief mulling a presidential bid. Unlikely: a kinetic clash or a major escalation in the next seven days.

North Korea: Possible that North Korea conducts another missile test or artillery exercise in the coming days, following the pattern of firing days after Kim's China visit. Unlikely: a new high-level meeting between the two leaders within the week.

Markets: Probable that Chinese A-share and HK-listed stocks remain volatile, with tech and semiconductor names in particular under pressure. Possible: a short-term rally if the government hints at stimulus, but the trend is downward. Almost certain that European auto stocks will continue to feel the China drag in their guidance updates.

Less likely surprises (possible but I would not bet on them): A sudden Chinese announcement of a large domestic stimulus package (say, a 2-trillion-yuan bond issuance) before the end of the week. A formal Chinese trade complaint to the WTO over the FCC or biotech bans within seven days. A new Chinese AI model release or chip breakthrough that shifts the global AI narrative. A diplomatic meeting between Xi and a Western leader (beyond the already-scheduled German and Swiss contacts) within the week.

Things I would not bet on: A major Chinese military exercise or live-fire drill in the Taiwan Strait within the next seven days. A full US–China trade negotiation or summit announcement. A change in China's one-child-successor demographic policy or a new baby-bonus announcement. A significant shift in China's stance on the South China Sea arbitration or a new territorial claim. A Chinese central-bank emergency rate cut of more than 10 basis points. A major natural disaster (typhoon, earthquake) hitting eastern China in the next week, though Tropical Storm Champi just passed, so the season is winding down.
emoji_reasons: The Mbappé–Mao scandal and the Sanrio/Hello Kitty cultural spat turned China into a stage where foreign celebrities and brands were publicly humiliated, making the drama of the week feel more like a soap opera than a news cycle.

Factory output contracted for the third time in four months, four major European automakers cut their outlooks on China weakness, and Chinese investors fled into bonds, painting a picture of a deepening economic slump.

The Communist Party plenum expelled a record 33 officials, elevated a purge general to the Politburo, and Xi demanded tighter discipline, making internal party politics the defining governance story of the week.

delta.motion: Between the two photographs, the most dramatic growth is in US-China tech and trade friction. A week earlier the story was a proposed Treasury rule and a DeepSeek government ban; by the second photo the FCC had banned all Chinese test labs, three genomics firms were out, telecom access was being cut, truck trailers faced tariffs, and a spy plot at Nvidia had Trump saying the US was looking closely. The escalation went from one sector to many and from proposals to votes. The economic malaise also grew sharply and became more visible globally. The first photo showed a 4.5 percent GDP print and a 10-week stock slide; the second shows the PMI contracting for a third time in four months, Volkswagen posting its deepest loss since Dieselgate, Audi and Mercedes cutting outlooks, Toyota falling for the eighth straight month, and analysts openly calling for a Japan-style stimulus. The pain migrated from abstract market data to named Western brands bleeding money. The party-discipline theme grew from early reporting about an upcoming plenum into a concrete, dramatic event: 33 officials expelled in a single session, a general elevated to the Politburo, and Xi demanding loyalty. The purge went from rumor to record. Maritime and border tensions grew in scale, from 16 Chinese ships and a coast guard monitoring a Philippine vessel to 50 ships in a wide sweep, combat-readiness patrols, data collection, and India approving 22 billion in military spending partly in response. The Chinese auto industry's domestic-demand crisis grew from a forecast (Volvo CEO saying the market was gone) to a confirmed reality (BYD and Geely running out of buyers, offsetting with exports). What shrank was the Tropical Storm Champi narrative, which was a major expected event in the first photo and is nearly invisible in the second, suggesting it passed without the disruption forecast. The specific DeepSeek drama faded; it was the dominant AI story in photo one and a background note in photo two, replaced by a broader AI landscape including CXMT's first profit, an AI model conducting cyberattacks, and Meta building a robot with Fourier. The Kim Jong Un visit, a headline diplomatic event in the first photo, became a footnote in the second, overshadowed by a North Korean missile test that followed. The Evergrande saga shrank from an open wound (1 percent recovery, two and a half years of grinding) to a smaller resolution (the property-management arm sold to a PE firm for 514 million). What appeared fresh in the second photo includes the Mbappé-Mao scandal, which dominated the cultural and media cycle and had no counterpart in the first; the Nvidia spy plot; the China-Switzerland trade accord and the upgraded China-Peru deal; the Sanrio spy-drama fallout; CXMT's first quarterly profit; China's first wheat inquiry to the US since the Trump-Xi summit; and Chinese investors fleeing equities for long-bond ETFs and watching junk dollar bonds have their worst week in a year. What vanished from the headlines includes the Citi license (resolved, no longer a story), the specific AI-token micro-drama question, the nursery-poisoning case, the FBI spy arrest, the wealthy-Chinese-offshore-money story, and the specific rare-earth squeeze narrative that had Japan as its focus. The overall speed of change was fast on the friction and purge axes but slow on the stimulus and structural-reform axes, with the economic pain deepening gradually rather than in a single shock.
delta.wind: The single most important expected event, the Communist Party plenum, happened as scheduled but delivered a different message than forecast. The expectation was a probable modest shift toward stimulus and consumer support, with the communiqué being parsed for economic signals. In reality the plenum was dominated by party discipline: 33 expulsions, the elevation of a general to the Politburo, and Xi demanding loyalty. The economic stimulus signal was secondary or absent. The expectation was wrong on the character of the event: it was a political consolidation, not an economic pivot. Tropical Storm Champi was expected to be almost certain to affect China and possibly disrupt ports and shipping. In the second photo the storm is barely a presence, suggesting it passed with less impact than the forecast implied. The expectation over-weighted its news significance. The Kim Jong Un follow-up was expected to produce diplomatic messaging, with a joint statement possible. The visit did generate follow-up, but the more notable event was a North Korean missile test days later, which was not in the expectation. The stock-market expectation was that the plenum would provide a short-term sentiment boost, with the bear market possibly extending if stimulus was insufficient. In reality the boost did not materialize; tech stocks sold off, investors fled to bonds, and junk dollar bonds had their worst week in a year. The plenum's disciplinary focus did not help markets, and the expectation was wrong on the direction of the catalyst. The US-China AI rivalry was expected to see at least one new policy move, with a DeepSeek or MiniMax announcement possible. The reality far exceeded this: the FCC lab ban, the biotech deal limits, three genomics bans, the telecom access restriction, the truck-trailer tariffs, the Nvidia spy plot, China's own AI export curbs, and an AI model conducting cyberattacks all landed in a single week. The expectation was directionally right but dramatically understated in scale and breadth. The EU-China 'China Shock 2.0' talks were expected to produce a working-level meeting focused on a specific sector. Instead, the trade diplomacy was broader and more bilateral: Xi met German leadership, Steinmeier visited Beijing, China signed a trade accord with Switzerland, and the China-Peru deal was upgraded. The EU-specific narrative was less prominent than expected, and the expectation had the wrong geographic focus. The rare-earth and mineral squeeze was expected to generate at least one commodity headline. The specific rare-earth story faded, and the commodity friction showed up in broader forms: the wheat inquiry, the truck-trailer tariffs, and the biotech bans. The expectation was roughly right that trade friction would continue but wrong on the specific commodity vehicle. The pharma and biotech expectation of one or two deals was met and slightly exceeded: Bayer got a stroke-drug approval, Swiss firms boosted drug investment, and China's cheap-trial model upended global drug development. The sector was more prominent than the 'unlikely to be a headline driver' caveat suggested, though it still did not dominate. The Mbappé-Mao scandal was entirely unexpected and became the single most-covered story of the week, a cultural-diplomatic event that no forecast anticipated. The Nvidia spy plot was a specific surprise that fed the broader AI-competition narrative in a way the expectation had not captured. The 33-official expulsion was more dramatic than the 'tougher internal discipline' early reporting suggested. The Sanrio spy-drama fallout was another cultural irritant that appeared from nowhere. What did not come, as the expectation correctly predicted: no full US-China trade truce, no major live-fire drill in the Taiwan Strait (the 50-ship sweep was notable but not a new exercise), no dramatic break from the economic model at the plenum, no new space launch dominating the news, no new Evergrande-scale property default, and no multi-year yuan move. The overall pattern of the expectation's errors is a consistent underestimation of the US's willingness to escalate across multiple sectors simultaneously and an overestimation of the plenum's economic signaling. The expectation also missed the cultural-diplomatic dimension entirely, which turned out to be the week's loudest story. For China specifically, the forecasting bias has been to treat the economy as the primary lens and the party as a background actor, when in practice the party's internal dynamics and China's cultural-soft-power reactions are now generating more headline volume than the GDP numbers.
delta.driver: The force pushing China from the first photograph to the second is the collision between internal consolidation and external economic pressure, played out in a week where the party tightened its grip just as the economy showed it is losing its domestic engine. The plenum's 33 expulsions and the elevation of a loyalist general to the Politburo signal that Xi is reshaping the leadership pipeline through the purge, prioritizing loyalty and discipline over the technocratic consensus that once defined the Politburo. At the same time, the PMI contraction, the Western auto brands' losses, and the BYD-Geely buyer shortage show that the domestic-demand weakness that was a footnote in the Q3 GDP report is now the main story, and the party's answer so far is not a large stimulus but a tightening of control and a push for exports and self-reliance. The US is escalating across the board, from test labs to biotech to telecom to truck trailers, and China is responding with its own export curbs, diplomatic outreach to Europe, and a willingness to punish foreign brands culturally, as the Mbappé episode showed. The underlying tension is that the party wants to consolidate power and demand loyalty internally while the economy needs confidence, spending, and open trade externally, and the two impulses are pulling in opposite directions. The Mbappé story, the Nvidia spy plot, and the 50-ship maritime sweep are all symptoms of the same thing: a China that is more confident in its leverage, more willing to test boundaries, and more sensitive to perceived slights, even as its domestic consumer is quietly retreating. The week's motion is not a single shock but the steady acceleration of a multi-front contest in which the party's internal discipline and the economy's external vulnerability are increasingly entangled.

judgment.reading_a: Forecast A delivered a broad, multi-threaded picture of the week and got the structural skeleton largely right. It correctly identified the Fifth Plenum as a dominant story and predicted the emphasis on internal discipline, consolidation of Xi's authority, and the anti-corruption push. The actual outcome of 33 record expulsions, the elevation of Zhang Shengmin to the Politburo, and the loyalty demands all fit A's framework. A expected 'at least a qualitative stimulus signal' from the plenum, which was partially confirmed; the meeting leaned more toward discipline than stimulus, so A slightly over-weighted the economic signal. A's US-China AI rivalry thread was well calibrated: it expected incremental two-way friction rather than a dramatic break, and the week delivered exactly that with the FCC ban on Chinese test labs, the Treasury's biotech curbs, the three genomics bans, the telecom phone-number ban, truck-trailer tariffs, China's retaliation warning, and the small thaw of the US wheat inquiry. A's prediction of 'at least one new Chinese counter-measure' was confirmed multiple times over. A's maritime and Taiwan thread was on target: the 50-vessel sweep, the combat-readiness patrols around the disputed shoal, and the Philippines-China tensions at ASEAN all matched A's expectation of 'sustained low-level friction, not escalation.' A's cyber-espionage cluster (FBI spy arrests, US device blocks, Japan rare-earth concerns) was broadly confirmed, though the specific Nvidia spy-plot story was not named. A's market predictions were directionally right: the AI-stock sell-off continued, the CSI 300 slide extended, Evergrande's property-management arm was sold to PAG for $514 million, and investors rotated into long-bond ETFs. A's North Korea thread was correct: the Kim Dandong visit generated follow-up coverage, and the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral was in 'preparation' mode (Zelenskyy was 'irked' by it). A's storm prediction was partially right: Tropical Storm Champi did approach China after battering Taiwan and Japan, but it was a secondary story rather than the compound-disaster narrative A anticipated. A's EU-China trade thread was less confirmed: the specific hybrid-vehicle tariff numbers and sector-by-sector negotiations A expected did not dominate, though the broader 'China Shock 2.0' framing persisted through the German and Swiss diplomacy. A's 'less likely surprises' list was largely accurate: the Chinese counter-ban on US tech (FCC lab ban) materialized, the DeepSeek IPO did not complete, and there was no dramatic V-shaped market reversal. What A missed most significantly was the Mbappé-Mao scandal, which was the single most-covered story of the week across at least a dozen outlets. A had no thread for sports, culture, or celebrity as a vector for Chinese soft-power enforcement. A also missed the Nvidia spy-plot specifically, the German Steinmeier visit and Xi's 'pragmatic policy' push, the China-Switzerland trade accord, the CXMT first-profit and AI-memory production story, the clean-tech exports and emissions impact, the Hello Kitty/Sanrio incident, the India-China border face-offs and India's $22 billion military spending, the Meta-Fourier humanoid robot, the Chinese AI model cyberattacks, the Bayer stroke-drug approval, and the US wheat inquiry as a thaw signal. A also slightly over-weighted the Tibet earthquake and storm as a compound-disaster narrative; the earthquake had already occurred and the storm was a secondary item. Overall, A's picture was structurally sound and its specific predictions were more often confirmed than not, but the #1 story of the week was entirely absent from its framework.
judgment.reading_b: Forecast B was more concise and hit the major structural notes but with less granularity. It correctly identified the Plenum as the 'single most important event' and predicted emphasis on qualitative growth, technological self-reliance, and internal discipline, all of which were confirmed. B expected 'a modest shift toward more stimulus and consumer support,' which was partially right; the plenum was more discipline-focused than stimulus-focused, so B slightly over-read the economic signal, similar to A. B's Tropical Storm Champi prediction was well placed: the storm did approach China's coast after hitting Taiwan and Japan, though it was a secondary story rather than a dominant one. B's Kim Jong Un thread was accurate: the Dandong visit generated follow-up coverage, the new cross-border bridge was inaugurated, and North Korea fired missiles days later. B correctly framed this in the US-China-Russia triangle context, and the Zelenskyy-irked-by-trilateral headline confirms the trilateral was in active preparation. B's stock-market prediction was directionally right: the plenum did not produce a relief rally, the AI-stock losses continued, and the bear market extended. B's US-China AI rivalry thread was on target, predicting 'at least one new US or Chinese AI-related policy move,' which materialized in multiple forms (FCC lab ban, biotech curbs, genomics bans, telecom ban). B's EU-China trade thread was less confirmed this week; the specific working-level meeting and sector-by-sector negotiations B expected did not dominate, though the broader trade friction continued. B's rare-earth and mineral squeeze prediction was confirmed: copper was 'sold out everywhere,' Mongolian copper exports dropped due to China border restrictions, and the broader commodity pressure persisted. B's pharma and biotech thread was a notable strength: it predicted 'one or two additional pharma deals or approvals,' and the week delivered the Bayer stroke-prevention drug approval in China and the broader 'China upends global drug development with cheap and rapid human trials' story. B also correctly noted this sector would not become a headline driver compared to AI and trade, which was accurate. B's 'less likely surprises' list was reasonable: no major new US sanction beyond what was already in motion, no second natural disaster, no sudden yuan shift. B's 'things I would not bet on' were all confirmed: no full trade truce, no dramatic Taiwan Strait exercise, no plenum policy break, no new space launch dominating the cycle, no new property developer default, no multi-year yuan extreme. What B missed was the same Mbappé-Mao scandal that A missed, plus the Nvidia spy-plot, the German and Swiss diplomacy specifics, the CXMT story, the clean-tech exports, the Hello Kitty incident, the India-China border tensions, the Meta-Fourier robot, the AI model cyberattacks, and the US wheat inquiry. B also did not mention the record expulsion of 33 officials or the Zhang Shengmin elevation, which were significant plenum details. B's treatment of the plenum was less specific than A's, missing the purge-and-consolidation angle that dominated the coverage. Overall, B's picture was directionally correct on most threads and its pharma and storm calls were more on target than A's, but it was less specific and less actionable as a reader's guide to the week.
judgment.comparison: Both forecasts shared the same core structure: the Plenum as a major domestic story, US-China tech and trade friction as the dominant bilateral thread, the stock market in a fragile bear phase, the Kim Jong Un visit as a diplomatic follow-up, and the Tropical Storm Champi as a near-term weather event. Both correctly identified the incremental, grinding nature of the US-China confrontation rather than a dramatic break, and both correctly expected the plenum to emphasize discipline and consolidation rather than a policy revolution. Both correctly predicted the market would not produce a V-shaped reversal. Both correctly anticipated the Kim visit follow-up and the trilateral meeting in preparation mode. Both correctly identified the maritime and Taiwan friction as sustained but not escalating. Both correctly expected the rare-earth and commodity pressure to persist. Both correctly noted the pharma sector as a relative bright spot (B more explicitly than A). Where both forecasts failed was the Mbappé-Mao scandal, the single most-covered story of the week. Neither forecast had a thread for sports, culture, or celebrity as a vector for Chinese soft-power enforcement, and the Sanrio/Hello Kitty incident that reinforced the same theme was also absent from both. This is a genuine surprise that is hard to predict from the prior week's headlines, but it dominated the news cycle to the point of eclipsing the plenum in global coverage, and a reader who relied on either forecast would have been unprepared for it. A second shared miss was the Nvidia spy-plot, which was a specific and high-profile story that neither forecast named, though A's broader cyber-espionage thread was closer to capturing the theme. The German Steinmeier visit, the China-Switzerland trade accord, and the CXMT first-profit story were also absent from both. In terms of specificity, A was more granular and provided more concrete 'what to watch for' items: the Citi securities unit, the sovereign wealth fund inflows, the DeepSeek IPO preparation, the MiniMax licensing, the HKEX AI indexes, the ConnectWise hack, the Webull data, the Japan rare-earth timeline, the BYD Brazil capacity, the Chery Canada plans, the China-Djibouti and South Africa deals, the sixteen-ship harassment operations, the transnational repression indictments, and the Citi launch. Many of these specific items were confirmed or partially confirmed, giving A a higher hit rate on granular predictions. B was more concise and its pharma thread was more on target, and its storm treatment was more prominent, but it offered fewer specific items to track. A's 'less likely surprises' list was more useful as a reader's checklist, and its 'what I would not bet on' list was more detailed. B's strength was readability and the correct elevation of pharma and the storm, but as a picture of the coming week, A's greater breadth and specificity would have served a reader better. A reader with A in hand would have had a more detailed map of the week's likely contours, with more specific items to confirm or deny. A reader with B in hand would have had a correct but thinner sketch. Both missed the #1 story, but A's additional threads (cyber, maritime specifics, market microstructure, North Korea diplomacy, EU trade specifics) gave it more surface area to intersect with the actual week. The edge goes to A for specificity and breadth, though the margin is not large because both captured the major structural themes and both missed the Mbappé scandal. VERDICT: A
